title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook
author: Jordan Li
body:
Overview

Purpose
This document consolidates our serving runtime reference material: architecture, kernel scheduling policies, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite, release notes summary, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers onboarding to the serving runtime, SREs, and product owners tracking runtime performance regressions.

Scope
- On-prem and hosted serving runtime components (router, dispatcher, worker, kv-cache, telemetry)
- Kernel and GPU scheduling policies used in production pools
- Profiling and triage playbook for performance incidents
- Benchmarking suite design and how to run reproducible experiments
- Recent release notes and prioritized known issues
- Runbooks for common operational tasks and incident response

Ownership
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (team)
- Doc owner: Jordan Li (author)

Architecture overview

High-level components
- Frontdoor / API Gateway: ingress for customer requests, performs authentication, rate limiting, and initial routing.
- Router: policy engine that selects model variant, pool, and schedule strategy (latency-first / cost-first / region-aware).
- Dispatcher: request batching/shard (per-GPU) coordinator that implements continuous batching and KV cache lookups.
- Worker (Inference Engine): GPU process hosting model shards, manages KV cache, executes optimized kernels.
- Metrics & Tracing: Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, token-level latency histograms, and per-request cost attribution.
- Control Plane: model catalog, rollout APIs, quantization profiles, and kernel selector service.

Sequence of a request (simplified)
1. Ingress receives request; validate auth and quota.
2. Router consults model catalog + routing policy; select pool and model variant.
3. Dispatcher checks prefix/KV cache; if hit return cached tokens or partial response.
4. Dispatcher groups compatible requests into batches (continuous batching) and dispatches to worker process.
5. Worker selects kernel path (FP16/INT8/optimized fused-attention) and executes.
6. Worker updates KV cache and returns token stream via router.
7. Metrics and traces emitted at each hop for post-hoc analysis.

Design goals and constraints
- Predictable latency (p95 < 200ms for short prompts on hosted tier)
- Cost efficiency via batching, caching, and quantization without significant quality regressions
- Transparent fallbacks (auto-fallback to compatible variants when capacity constrained)
- Observability for per-token cost and traceable regressions

Kernel scheduling and selection

Overview
The kernel selector chooses among multiple implementation variants for attention, softmax, matmuls, and KV cache management. Selection factors:
- Model architecture (transformer type, kv cache layout)
- Sequence length and temperature distribution
- Hardware characteristics (GPU model, SM count, memory bandwidth)
- Quantization profile (FP16, NF4/INT4)
- Concurrency level and memory pressure (active batches, cached entries)

Priority rules (production policy)
1. Hardware capability: prefer fused/fast kernels only on GPUs with known stability profiles (e.g., A100-80GB, H100).
2. Sequence-length aware selection: for seq_len <= 256 favor single-token fused kernels; for seq_len > 2048 use tiled/attention-chunked kernels.
3. Quantization guardrail: disable extreme quantization kernels for models with known degeneration profiles (see quantization-profiles doc).
4. Memory safety: if estimated GPU memory usage > 92% avoid large batch kernels and fall back to sequential kernels.

Kernel fallback matrix (simplified table)
Condition: A100, seq<=256, FP16 | Preferred kernel: fused-attn-v2 | Fallback kernel: tile-attn | Notes: fused-attn-v2 gives best throughput
Condition: H100, seq>1024, INT8 | Preferred kernel: chunked-attn | Fallback kernel: tile-attn | Notes: chunked-attn reduces memory peaks
Condition: GPU mem>92% | Preferred kernel: sequential-attn | Fallback kernel: none | Notes: avoids OOM but increases latency

Profiling playbook (incident triage)

When latency or error rates exceed SLOs follow this playbook. Primary triage owner: on-call serving-runtime SRE.

1) Collect context (first 5 minutes)
- Confirm alert: check Grafana dashboard for p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, queue length, and GPU utilization.
- Pull traces: use OpenTelemetry traces filtered by route/model id.
- Identify scope: single pool, region, specific model, or global.

2) Quick checks (5-15 minutes)
- Check recent deploys: control plane change, model rollout, kernel selection changes, quantization profile updates (control-plane audit).
- Check GPU errors: dmesg and NVIDIA driver logs on affected hosts for ECC, Xid or thermal events.
- Verify KV cache hit-rate: low hit-rate often increases compute.

3) Deeper profiling (15-45 minutes)
- Reproduce with perf-runner: run a workload from the benchmarking suite that matches the failing route.
- Collect per-kernel timelines with CUPTI / Nsight sampling.
- Record memory allocation timelines and fragmentation using our mem-tracer tool.

4) Mitigations (while investigating)
- Rollback recent control-plane change or pin model to previous variant.
- Scale up pool capacity (add machines to dedicated pool) and temporarily switch routing policy to less-costly but faster pool.
- Adjust batching window: reduce max batch size if excessive queuing causing head-of-line blocking.

5) Postmortem
- Document root cause, mitigations, and action items in incident postmortem template.
- If kernel bug: create issue in runtime-kernels repo with CUPTI traces and minimal repro.

Benchmarking suite (reproducible performance experiments)

Goals
- Produce stable, repeatable benchmarks for throughput, latency, and cost-per-token across model variants and hardware.
- Provide a standardized harness for regression testing on PRs and release candidates.

Components
- workloads/: YAML-driven workload definitions (prompt sets, parallel clients, arrival distributions).
- runner/: tools to run workloads against a local or staging pool; supports both synthetic and recorded request replays.
- metrics-collector/: collects Prometheus metrics, GPU traces, and token-attribution logs; outputs a standardized JSON report.

How to run a canonical benchmark (example)
1. Checkout repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/serving-bench.git
2. Select workload: workloads/long-context-rlhf.yml
3. Run:
./runner/run.py --workload workloads/long-context-rlhf.yml --pool staging-a100 --duration 15m --out report.json

4. Postprocess:
./metrics-collector/compare.py report.json baseline-2026-01-10.json --out delta-report.html

Benchmark result fields (report.json)
- mean_latency_ms, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms
- throughput_tps, tokens_per_second, cost_per_token_usd
- kernel-level utilization and per-kernel tail latencies

Release notes (summary of recent runtime releases)

2026-02-10 (v2.14.0) - production rollout
- Kernel selector: added H100 chunked-attn optimization (10-15% throughput improvement on long contexts).
- Memory tracer integrated into worker builds for better OOM triage.
- Default routing policy: prefer high-availability pools for enterprise customers.

2025-12-02 (v2.12.4) - hotfix
- Fixed race in continuous batching that could drop requests under high concurrency.
- Backported improved quantization guardrails for NF4 models.

Known issues (priority ordered)
- KRN-1287: Occasional Xid 61 on H100 machines under mixed FP16+INT8 workloads. Workaround: set environment var RW_DISABLE_INT8_MIX=1. (Owner: infra/gpu-fleet)
- KRN-1312: Degraded KV cache hit-rate after large model rollout due to mismatch in prefix normalization. Fix in progress (expected 2026-03). (Owner: eng-serving-runtime)
- KRN-1401: Rare multi-batch head-of-line blocking when max_batch_size is high and arrival skew is extreme. Mitigation: reduce max_batch_size to 32 for affected pools. (Owner: eng-platform)

Runtime runbooks (common operational tasks)

A) Scale up a dedicated GPU pool (for urgent capacity)
1. Navigate to Console -> Pools -> affected-pool -> Actions -> Add nodes.
2. Select template: pool-a100-large; replica count +3.
3. Confirm autoscaler behavior: set cooldown to 5m for temporary bursts.
4. Monitor: p95 latency and queuing metrics for 10 minutes.

B) Rollback a kernel selector change
1. Identify change in control-plane audit and obtain rollout id.
2. In control plane: rollback rollout or pin model_variant to previous tag.
3. Run smoke tests from runner/ smoke.yml to validate request flow.
4. If issue persists, escalate to runtime-kernels on-call with CUPTI traces.

C) Reproduce a latency regression locally
1. Use perf-runner to replay recorded requests matching the route id.
2. Toggle kernel selection flags in the local worker binary and re-run.
3. Collect nsight/cupti timelines and attach to ticket.

Team wiki & onboarding notes

- Quickstart: clone serving-runtime repo, build dev-worker with `make dev-worker`, and run `./dev-run --pool local`.
- Useful links:
  - Runtime CI: https://ci.internal.redwood/runtime
  - Kernel selector docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling
  - Benchmarking repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/serving-bench.git

SLOs and alerting thresholds (production hosted tier)
- Request success rate: >= 99.9% (5m window)
- p95 latency (short prompts, <256 tokens): <= 200ms
- p99 latency: <= 500ms
- Queue length warning: > 50 requests pending for 1 minute
- GPU mem pressure alert: utilization > 92% for 3 minutes

Appendix: diagnostic commands and examples
- Check pool status (CLI):
rwctl pool list --region us-west-2 --format table
rwctl pool inspect affected-pool --json > pool.json

- Collect driver logs from host (example):
ssh gpu-host-12 'sudo journalctl -u nvidia-driver.service --since "1 hour ago" > /tmp/driver.log'
scp gpu-host-12:/tmp/driver.log ./driver.log

- Run quick perf:
./runner/run.py --workload workloads/short-chat.yml --pool local --duration 2m --concurrency 8

Contacts and escalation
- Primary on-call: eng-sre rota (see roster)
- Kernel bugs: runtime-kernels on-call (pager duty: runtime-kernels)
- GPU infra incidents: infra/gpu-fleet lead (Marco Hernandez)
